records.title: kggraph: reify syntactic constructs as concept nodes (construct:* + custom:uses_* edges) — makes "where is X used?" a one-call graph query
records.body:
## Motivation

"Where are recursive CTEs used?" / "which procs use cursors?" / "where is dynamic SQL?" are construct-usage questions the kggraph cannot answer today: its vocabulary is relations between durable named objects (proc → table, method → proc), and a syntactic construct is a property of a definition body, not an identity. Today the only way to answer them is a regex scan over source.

Meanwhile the `dynamic_sql` signal is already detected and emitted — but as `facts`, which the trusty-search ingest endpoint drops (nodes+edges only, FactStore unwired). So our highest-value syntactic finding is currently produced and then lost.

## Proposal: construct concept nodes

Reify each syntactic construct as a namespaced concept node and emit one custom edge per using definition:

```json
{"id": "construct:recursive_cte", "kind": "construct"}
{"from": "dbo.qry_TreeWalk", "to": "construct:recursive_cte",
 "tag": "custom:uses_recursive_cte", "provenance": ["SQL/file.sql"]}
```

"Where are recursive CTEs used?" then becomes one call:

```
GET /indexes/{id}/graph/neighbors?node=construct:recursive_cte&direction=in&edge_kinds=custom:uses_recursive_cte
```

**Zero trusty-search changes required — validated live 2026-06-12** against daemon v0.24.4: ingested exactly the shape above under a scratch producer → accepted (`unknown_edge_tags_dropped: 0`, node kind `"construct"` round-tripped), neighbors query with `edge_kinds=custom:uses_recursive_cte` returned the proc with the custom label intact, empty-replace erased it. The `custom:` tag routes through `EdgeKind::from_tag` to `Custom(String)` (#818 escape hatch) and survives warm-boot (#816); free-form node kinds need no registration.

This is also an established trusty-tools idiom: trusty-memory's palace KG reifies `tag:` / `topic:` / `room:` subjects for exactly this clustering purpose (`trusty-memory/src/kg_extract.rs`), and the kggraph's own table nodes are the same move for resources.

## Initial construct vocabulary (keep it coarse — these become high-in-degree hub nodes)

| node id | detection (ScriptDom) |
|---|---|
| `construct:dynamic_sql` | existing detection — migrate the current `dynamic_sql` facts to edges |
| `construct:cursor` | `DeclareCursorStatement` / `FetchCursorStatement` |
| `construct:recursive_cte` | `CommonTableExpression` whose body references its own name (AST-accurate version of the self-reference check) |
| `construct:merge_statement` | `MergeStatement` |
| `construct:nolock_hint` | `TableHint` kind `NoLock` |

One edge per (definition, construct) pair regardless of occurrence count inside the body; occurrence files go in `provenance` (existing dedup/merge machinery handles this).

## Notes

- `--emit edges` (default mode) unchanged; constructs appear only in `--emit kggraph`.
- Byte-determinism preserved: constructs are a pure function of the parsed AST; ordinal node/edge ordering as today.
- Keep the `dynamic_sql` facts in the output for now (back-compat) — or drop them in the same change if nothing consumes them; either way the edge form becomes the queryable representation.
- C# pass could later join in (e.g. `construct:raw_sql_concatenation`), but T-SQL-only is a fine first slice.
- Orthogonal to #6 (identity seam): construct edges originate from T-SQL-pass definitions, which are already schema-qualified.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `--emit kggraph` emits `construct:*` nodes (kind `construct`) + `custom:uses_*` edges per the table above
- [ ] `dynamic_sql` detection reachable via `construct:dynamic_sql` edges
- [ ] Output remains byte-deterministic (existing test pattern)
- [ ] Live check: ingest pilot doc, `graph/neighbors?node=construct:dynamic_sql&direction=in` returns the flagged procs

records.title: feat: depends_on should be wait-until-ready, not just start-order
records.body:
## Problem

\`depends_on = [\"backend\"]\` in \`service.toml\` currently guarantees start-order (backend container is created + started before frontend), but **not** readiness — the backend can be in any state between \"docker started\" and \"actually serving traffic\" when the frontend boots.

That's fine for most services that themselves retry, but a large class of container entrypoints does one-shot DNS resolution at boot (nginx configs with \`proxy_pass http://backend:8000\`, envoy configs with static clusters, some database driver connect-strings) — a boot-time TCP or DNS failure kills the process and, combined with \`restart=no\` (see orca#121), leaves the service dead.

Compose has this same problem and papered over it with \`depends_on: condition: service_healthy\` requiring the depended-on service to have a healthcheck. Kubernetes solved it with readiness probes gating init containers.

## Repro

Real incident 2026-07-07, cluster \`breakpilot\`:

1. Something triggers a mass container recreate on the agent \`ubuntu-16gb-fsn1-1\` (in our case it was orca#120's reconcile scope bleed).
2. Orca starts \`erp-backend\` at 07:46:17 UTC. Docker registers its network alias asynchronously.
3. Orca starts \`erp-frontend\` at 07:46:16 UTC (per \`depends_on = [\"erp-backend\"]\`).

   **Note the second: frontend started 1 second BEFORE backend.** \`depends_on\` was violated. In our case both were on the same agent, launched by the same orca-agent process, and yet the ordering wasn't enforced.
4. nginx in erp-frontend does a config parse; \`proxy_pass http://erp-backend:8000\` → \`getaddrinfo(\"erp-backend\")\` → \`[emerg] host not found in upstream\`. Process exits.
5. Container marked \`restart=no\`. Service dead.

Even if orca had honored strict start-order, the DNS alias would have taken another few hundred ms to propagate through Docker's embedded DNS. That's a race, not a start-order fix.

## Proposed API

\`\`\`toml
[[service]]
name = \"erp-frontend\"
depends_on = [\"erp-backend\"]     # existing: start-order-ish
wait_for = [                       # NEW: block start until reachable
    \"erp-backend:tcp:8000\",       # TCP connect
    \"erp-db:tcp:3306:30s\",        # with timeout
    \"erp-backend:http:/health\",    # HTTP 200
]
\`\`\`

Or richer:

\`\`\`toml
[[service.wait_for]]
target = \"erp-backend\"
check = \"tcp\"
port = 8000
timeout = \"30s\"

[[service.wait_for]]
target = \"erp-db\"
check = \"http\"
path = \"/health\"
port = 8000
expect_status = 200
\`\`\`

Semantics: orca launches the container only after every \`wait_for\` check passes. Implementation-wise this can be a tiny sidecar (\`orca-wait\`) that runs before the real entrypoint, or a wrapper around the entrypoint command orca injects, or a real orca-agent-side pre-flight check.

**Compat:** \`depends_on\` keeps its current start-order semantic. \`wait_for\` is additive.

## Alternatives considered

- **Wrap every entrypoint with a wait-loop.** What we did as a workaround (\`sh -c 'until getent hosts backend; do sleep 1; done; exec entrypoint'\`). Works, but every service operator has to remember to do it, and the loop needs to be written per-service depending on what constitutes \"ready\" (DNS resolvable? TCP open? HTTP 200 on /health?).
- **Rely on the restart_policy from orca#121.** Restart-on-failure fixes many symptoms but doesn't address the actual race — a service can crash-loop indefinitely if the retry timing collides with the backend's readiness window. Wait-for-ready is the semantic fix; restart-policy is the safety net.
- **Kubernetes-style pod readinessProbes.** Would need to model probe results in orca's status API. Bigger change than \`wait_for\` at the depends_on level.

## Trade-offs

- Adds a small runtime dependency (either an injected wrapper or an orca-agent pre-flight check).
- If a \`wait_for\` target never becomes ready, the depending container never starts. Orca needs a clear \"stuck waiting\" state distinct from \"crashed\" in \`orca status\`.
- Circular waits should be a validation error at deploy time.

## Related

- [orca#120](https://github.com/mighty840/orca/issues/120) — reconcile scope bleed (the trigger that exposed this).
- [orca#121](https://github.com/mighty840/orca/issues/121) — restart-policy support (the safety net that would mask this from becoming outages).
- [orca#119](https://github.com/mighty840/orca/issues/119) — cluster-native status page (would detect these earlier).

Together, #119 + #120 + #121 + this issue = the reconcile/startup hardening pass.

---
🤖 Filed via Claude Code

records.title: Security: Transitive dependencies with known vulnerabilities in @modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.29.0
records.body:
## Summary

`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.29.0` ships with transitive dependencies that have known security vulnerabilities. Downstream consumers running `npm audit --audit-level=high` get a non-zero exit code, breaking CI pipelines.

## Affected dependencies

| Package | Installed | Fixed | Severity | Advisory |
|---------|-----------|-------|----------|----------|
| `fast-uri` | 3.1.0 (via `ajv@8.18.0`) | ≥3.1.2 | **high** | [GHSA-q3j6-qgpj-74h6](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q3j6-qgpj-74h6), [GHSA-v39h-62p7-jpjc](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v39h-62p7-jpjc) |
| `hono` | 4.12.14 | ≥4.12.18 | moderate | [GHSA-9vqf-7f2p-gf9v](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9vqf-7f2p-gf9v), [GHSA-69xw-7hcm-h432](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-69xw-7hcm-h432), [GHSA-qp7p-654g-cw7p](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qp7p-654g-cw7p), [GHSA-hm8q-7f3q-5f36](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hm8q-7f3q-5f36), [GHSA-p77w-8qqv-26rm](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p77w-8qqv-26rm) |
| `ip-address` | 10.1.0 (via `express-rate-limit@8.4.0`) | ≥10.2.0 | moderate | [GHSA-v2v4-37r5-5v8g](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v2v4-37r5-5v8g) |
| `express-rate-limit` | 8.4.0 | ≥8.5.1 | moderate | Depends on vulnerable `ip-address` |

## Dependency chain

```
@modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.29.0
├── ajv@8.18.0
│   └── fast-uri@3.1.0          ← HIGH: path traversal, host confusion
├── hono@4.12.14                ← moderate: bodyLimit bypass, JSX injection, JWT validation, cache leakage
├── @hono/node-server@1.19.14
│   └── hono@4.12.14 (deduped)
└── express-rate-limit@8.4.0
    └── ip-address@10.1.0       ← moderate: XSS in Address6
```

## Reproduction

```bash
mkdir repro && cd repro
npm init -y
npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk@1.29.0
npm audit --audit-level=high
# Exit code: 1
```

## Suggested fix

All existing semver ranges in the SDK's `package.json` already allow the fixed versions. A lockfile regeneration or minimum version bump in `package.json` resolves all four:

```jsonc
// package.json (suggested minimum version bumps)
{
  "dependencies": {
    "ajv": "^8.18.0",              // fast-uri ^3.0.1 resolves to 3.1.2 ✓
    "hono": "^4.12.18",           // was ^4.11.4
    "express-rate-limit": "^8.5.1" // was ^8.2.1, pulls ip-address ≥10.2.0
  }
}
```

No breaking changes — all fixes are patch/minor semver-compatible.

## Impact

Any downstream project with `npm audit` in CI (standard security practice) fails on `--audit-level=high` due to `fast-uri`. This blocks releases and forces consumers to add `overrides` as a workaround.

## Workaround (for downstream consumers)

```jsonc
// package.json
{
  "overrides": {
    "fast-uri": ">=3.1.2",
    "hono": ">=4.12.18",
    "ip-address": ">=10.2.0",
    "express-rate-limit": ">=8.5.1"
  }
}
```

## Environment

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`: 1.29.0 (latest as of 2025-05-11)
- Node.js: 22.x
- npm: 10.x
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 (CI), macOS 15 (local)

records.title: [Feature]: Workflow Orchestration
records.body:
### Deployment type

Self-hosted

### What do you want and why?

下面是一版可以直接提交到 issue / feature request 的双语版本。

---

## 中文版

**标题：希望 Multica 支持内置 Workflow 编排能力，用于更可控地管理多 Agent 协作流程**

### 背景

Multica 目前已经将 Agent 作为一等公民，支持 Agent 参与任务、评论、状态流转和协作。但在实际使用多 Agent 协作时，目前还缺少一个明确的 workflow 编排层，用来控制多个 Agent 任务之间的执行顺序、条件分支、审批节点、失败重试和状态流转。

当一个复杂任务需要多个 Agent 分工协作时，例如 PM Agent、Research Agent、Coding Agent、Review Agent、QA Agent 依次参与，当前的流程控制主要依赖人为约定或外部工具，整体可控性不足。

### 当前解决方案及问题

目前可以通过几种方式实现类似能力：

1. 使用一个 PMO / Coordinator Agent Skill 来维护流程状态机  
   问题是 skill 约束不够强，更多依赖 prompt 和 agent 自觉执行，流程状态容易失控。

2. 使用轮询机制控制任务流转  
   问题是实现复杂，效率较低，也不够直观。

3. 借助 n8n、飞书工作流等外部流程工具，通过 webhook、CLI 或 API 调度 Multica  
   问题是跨服务配置复杂，调试成本高，团队需要维护额外系统。

### Feature Request

希望未来 Multica 可以提供一个内置的 **Workflow section / Workflow builder**，用于编排多 Agent 协作流程。

目标能力可以类似 n8n 或飞书工作流，通过节点和连线定义任务流转：

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["任务创建"] --> B["PM Agent 拆解需求"]
    B --> C{"是否需要调研？"}
    C -- 是 --> D["Research Agent 输出调研结论"]
    C -- 否 --> E["Coding Agent 实现"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Review Agent 代码审查"]
    F --> G{"审查是否通过？"}
    G -- 否 --> E
    G -- 是 --> H["QA Agent 验证"]
    H --> I{"验证是否通过？"}
    I -- 否 --> E
    I -- 是 --> J["任务完成"]
```

### 期望能力

希望 Workflow 能支持：

- 节点配置：每个节点可以绑定 Agent、Skill、CLI 命令、Webhook 或人工审批。
- 条件网关：支持 if / else、审批通过 / 不通过、测试通过 / 失败等强条件控制。
- 状态机约束：流程状态由 workflow 引擎控制，而不是只依赖 Agent 自行遵守。
- 多 Agent 协作：不同 Agent 可以在不同节点承担明确职责。
- 失败处理：支持 retry、fallback、timeout、人工接管。
- 可视化追踪：可以看到当前流程执行到哪个节点、谁在处理、为什么阻塞。
- 与 Issue 集成：workflow 可以绑定到 issue、project、template 或 workspace 级别。
- 事件触发：支持 issue 创建、状态变更、评论、Agent 输出、CI 结果等事件触发流程。

### 价值

这个能力可以让 Multica 从“AI-native task management”进一步扩展到“AI-native workflow orchestration”。

它可以显著提升多 Agent 协作的可控性，减少 prompt-based 协调的不确定性，也降低接入外部自动化工具的复杂度。

核心价值是：  
**让 Agent 协作不只是靠对话和约定，而是由可视化、可审计、强约束的 workflow 来驱动。**

---

## English Version

**Title: Add Native Workflow Orchestration for More Controlled Multi-Agent Collaboration**

### Background

Multica already treats agents as first-class citizens. Agents can be assigned issues, comment, update status, and participate in team workflows. However, Multica currently lacks a native workflow orchestration layer for controlling how multiple agents collaborate across complex tasks.

In real-world multi-agent work, a task may involve several roles, such as a PM Agent, Research Agent, Coding Agent, Review Agent, and QA Agent. These agents often need to run in a specific order, branch based on conditions, retry on failure, or wait for approval before continuing.

At the moment, this flow is difficult to control reliably inside Multica.

### Current Workarounds and Limitations

There are a few possible workarounds today:

1. Use a PMO / Coordinator Agent Skill to manage the workflow state machine  
   The limitation is that skill-based constraints are not strong enough. The flow depends heavily on prompts and agent compliance.

2. Use polling-based orchestration  
   This works, but it is complex, inefficient, and hard to inspect.

3. Use external workflow tools such as n8n or Feishu Workflow via webhooks, CLI, or APIs  
   This provides stronger orchestration, but cross-service configuration is complicated and adds operational overhead.

### Feature Request

It would be valuable for Multica to provide a native **Workflow section / Workflow builder** for orchestrating multi-agent workflows.

The target experience could be similar to n8n or Feishu Workflow, where users define nodes, gateways, and transitions visually:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Issue Created"] --> B["PM Agent breaks down requirements"]
    B --> C{"Research needed?"}
    C -- Yes --> D["Research Agent prepares findings"]
    C -- No --> E["Coding Agent implements"]
    D --> E
    E --> F["Review Agent reviews code"]
    F --> G{"Review passed?"}
    G -- No --> E
    G -- Yes --> H["QA Agent verifies"]
    H --> I{"QA passed?"}
    I -- No --> E
    I -- Yes --> J["Issue Done"]
```

### Expected Capabilities

The workflow system could support:

- Node configuration: bind each node to an Agent, Skill, CLI command, Webhook, or human approval.
- Conditional gateways: support if / else logic, approval results, test results, review outcomes, and other strong transition rules.
- State machine enforcement: workflow state should be controlled by the workflow engine, not only by agent prompt discipline.
- Multi-agent collaboration: different agents can own clearly defined steps in the process.
- Failure handling: support retry, fallback, timeout, and manual takeover.
- Visual execution tracking: show the current node, owner, status, and blocking reason.
- Issue integration: attach workflows to issues, projects, templates, or workspace-level automation.
- Event triggers: start or continue workflows based on issue creation, status changes, comments, agent outputs, CI results, and other events.

### Value

This would help Multica evolve from an **AI-native task management platform** into an **AI-native workflow orchestration platform**.

The key value is to make multi-agent collaboration more reliable, observable, and controllable.

Instead of relying only on conversations, conventions, or prompt-based coordination, Multica could provide a visual, auditable, and strongly enforced workflow layer for agent collaboration.

### Proposed solution (optional)

_No response_

### Screenshots / mockups (optional)

_No response_

records.title: M06 — I35 Implement Experiment Planner, Runner, Execution Order, and Cell Registry

## Issue Summary

- **Milestone:** M06 — Collapse Experiments and Resolved Core
- **Primary deliverable:** Implement read-only planning, exact-name experiment execution, dependency-ordered workflow, semantic cell enumeration/counts, completion accounting, reuse/recovery, and invalid-baseline preservation.
- **Issue type:** Infrastructure / Implementation

## Roadmap Authority

### Roadmap Sections

- §24.3
- §24.5
- §29
- §30
- §31

### Requirements

- **Implementation requirements:** REQ-1537–REQ-1540; REQ-1545–REQ-1557; REQ-1760–REQ-1777; REQ-1780–REQ-1782; REQ-1914–REQ-1939; REQ-2203
- **Preserved non-implementation constraints:** REQ-1558; REQ-1778–REQ-1779
## Objective

Implement read-only planning, exact-name experiment execution, dependency-ordered workflow, semantic cell enumeration/counts, completion accounting, reuse/recovery, and invalid-baseline preservation.

## Scope

Implement only the following roadmap/inventory requirements. Each bullet is an explicit implementation obligation; none may remain implicit in tests or downstream work.

- **REQ-1537 — §24.3 — CLI / Execution:** `plan` must be read-only.
- **REQ-1538 — §24.3 — CLI / Execution:** `plan` must resolve canonical experiment order, dependencies, datasets, methods, conditions, seeds, Section 31 counts, blocked conditions, matched-reference prerequisites, and reusable artifact families.
- **REQ-1539 — §24.3 — CLI / Execution:** Before collapse completion, `plan` must show post-core cells as dependent on unresolved core; after all four decisions, it must show the mechanically derived core mapping.
- **REQ-1540 — §24.3 — CLI / Execution:** `plan` must not create a user-managed plan and must not accept overwrite.
- **REQ-1545 — §24.5 — CLI / Execution:** `run <experiment name>` must accept only exact descriptive Section 30 experiment names.
- **REQ-1546 — §24.5 — CLI / Execution:** One `run` invocation must own prerequisite validation, planned cell execution, metrics, statistical analysis, CIs/effects, multiplicity, scientific gates, invariant/provenance verification, and experiment completion.
- **REQ-1547 — §24.5 — Artifact:** Before each cell, `run` must resolve the artifact DAG and reuse matching data/splits/scalers/anchors/source/reproduction checkpoints/scores/calibrations/verifier/final-gate intermediates even across experiments.
- **REQ-1548 — §24.5 — Provenance:** Experiment identity may enter an artifact fingerprint only when the experiment definition changes the artifact's scientific semantics.
- **REQ-1549 — §24.5 — CLI / Execution:** Once the fourth collapse decision is complete, `run` must materialize/validate the deterministic Resolved FedSIRA Core artifact.
- **REQ-1550 — §24.5 — Failure Semantics:** Post-core experiments must refuse execution when the Resolved FedSIRA Core prerequisite is absent or stale.
- **REQ-1551 — §24.5 — Artifact:** A later cell failure must not invalidate already completed independent cells or shared upstream artifacts.
- **REQ-1552 — §24.5 — Artifact:** After correction, `run` must recompute only the first affected artifact and descendants; metric corrections may reuse scores, scoring corrections checkpoints, training corrections prepared data/unaffected anchors, and reporting corrections all scientific computation.
- **REQ-1553 — §24.5 — CLI / Execution:** Analysis/statistics/protocol verification must be internal to `run`; there must be no separate public analysis/verification command.
- **REQ-1554 — §24.5 — Failure Semantics:** A scientifically unfavorable/null result must still complete as `Completed`; technical execution failure is `Failed`; leakage/invariant/provenance/authoritative-config violation is `Invalid`.
- **REQ-1555 — §24.5 — CLI / Execution:** If all required artifacts are already validly complete, `run` must return an already-completed success and create no duplicate observation.
- **REQ-1556 — §24.5 — CLI / Execution:** `run --overwrite` must recompute experiment-owned artifacts under the same scientific contract without recursively rebuilding compatible shared prerequisites.
- **REQ-1557 — §24.5 — Artifact:** Overwrite replacements must be staged and atomically activated; unchanged identity preserves descendants, changed identity stales only descendants.

- **REQ-1761 — §29 — CLI / Execution:** Execution order 2 must be `Preprocessing and data/domain validation` and may proceed only when `Sections 9–11 schema/identity/split/leakage/target/evidence feasibility and deterministic preprocessing checks pass`.

records.title: Limit maximum data resident in the DAG at any moment (credit-based admission control)
records.body:
## Overview

There is currently no way to bound the total amount of data resident in a DAG at any given
moment. For pipelines where each in-flight dataset holds a large intermediate footprint on
disk — and where that footprint is only released by a terminal cleanup node — the async
orchestrator reliably runs "top-heavy": nearly every dataset completes the first stage before
later stages meaningfully start, so peak storage scales with the *total* number of submitted
datasets rather than with cluster width.

### Motivating case

A 10-step pipeline, 300 datasets, each holding ~1TB of cache while in flight, released by a
terminal cleanup node. Ray autoscales to 25 workers. Submitting all 300 at once overruns
storage capacity, because ~300 datasets accumulate stage-1 cache before the cleanup node runs
for any of them.

### Why it happens

`AsyncPipelineOrchestrator` launches every node as a concurrent `asyncio.TaskGroup` task
(`src/orcapod/pipeline/async_orchestrator.py:181`). With no concurrency limit, node 1 drains
its input channel as fast as it fills and submits essentially all work to Ray immediately.
Ray schedules roughly FIFO, so all node-1 tasks occupy the worker slots ahead of any node-2
task. The terminal cleanup node is last in the queue by construction.

The `SyncPipelineOrchestrator` is maximally top-heavy by design — it fully materializes each
node before starting the next (`src/orcapod/pipeline/sync_orchestrator.py:84-118`) — so this
feature is only meaningful for the async orchestrator.

### Why existing knobs don't solve it

- **Bounded channels** (`Channel(buffer_size=...)`, `src/orcapod/channels.py:157`) bound
  *queued* items on a single edge. They say nothing about how many items are simultaneously
  being worked on across all nodes.
- **`PodConfig.max_concurrency`** (`src/orcapod/core/function_pod.py:544-578`) is per-node.
  Setting `N` on each of 10 nodes still permits `10 × N` datasets in flight, and node 1 keeps
  admitting a new dataset the instant it retires one — which is precisely the failure mode.
- **`PipelineConfig.default_max_concurrency` is not plumbed through the pipeline path at all.**
  `AsyncPipelineOrchestrator` never accepts or forwards a `PipelineConfig` (it takes its own
  `buffer_size`/`error_policy`, `async_orchestrator.py:50-56`), and
  `FunctionJobNode.async_execute` calls `execution_pod.async_execute(...)` without one
  (`src/orcapod/core/nodes/function_node.py:2499`), so it silently falls back to
  `PipelineConfig()` → unlimited. `src/orcapod/pipeline/execution_context.py:20` still marks
  this integration as deferred. Today only `PodConfig.max_concurrency` set directly on the pod
  has any effect on the pipeline path.

## Proposed approach

Credit-based admission control (the same idea as Flink's credit-based flow control or Reactive
Streams `request(n)`): bound the number of items resident in the DAG, and release a credit when
an item exits.

Concretely, an `asyncio.Semaphore(N)` owned by the orchestrator:

1. Acquire a credit before a source node emits a dataset.
2. Release the credit when that dataset exits the DAG at a terminal node.

Both hook points are wrapper-shaped, so nodes need no changes — the existing `_CollectingWriter`
(`async_orchestrator.py:253`) is the exact pattern to follow. A new `PipelineConfig` field
(e.g. `max_datasets_in_flight: int | None = None`) would expose it, which also gives a reason
to finally plumb `PipelineConfig` into the orchestrator.

This stays fully async — there is no barrier. The moment dataset 1 finishes cleanup, dataset
N+1 is admitted, so pipelining across stages is preserved and workers stay saturated. The
synchronous alternative (submit in fixed chunks, wait for each chunk to fully drain) is
strictly worse because every chunk pays for its slowest dataset.

## Goals & Success Criteria

* A pipeline-level configuration option caps the number of datasets simultaneously resident
  in the DAG.
* With the cap set to `N`, peak concurrent in-flight datasets never exceeds `N`, regardless of
  how many datasets are submitted.
* Throughput is not barrier-limited: a new dataset is admitted as soon as any in-flight dataset
  exits, not only when a whole batch completes.
* Credits are released on **every** exit path, not just the happy one (see Risks).
* Existing pipelines with the cap unset behave exactly as they do today.

## Scope & Boundaries

In scope:
* Async orchestrator only.
* Credit accounting for the linear, single-terminal-node case.
* Plumbing `PipelineConfig` into `AsyncPipelineOrchestrator` (currently unwired).

Out of scope (candidates for follow-up issues):
* Sync orchestrator — top-heavy by construction; the gate is not meaningful there.
* Byte-aware admission (capping on actual bytes-on-disk rather than dataset count). Dataset
  count is a reasonable first proxy.
* Fan-out/fan-in lineage refcounting, if it proves large enough to split out — see below.

## Dependencies & Risks

* **Leaked credits deadlock the pipeline.** This is the main correctness hazard. A row can
  leave the DAG without reaching a terminal node: a data function returning `None` filters the
  item (handled at `src/orcapod/core/nodes/function_node.py:2442-2476`), and a crashed item is
  swallowed and never forwarded (`src/orcapod/core/function_pod.py:561-566`). Release must be
  tied to "left the DAG by any means," not "reached the terminal node." Get this wrong and the
  pipeline hangs permanently at `N` in-flight. This deserves more design care than the
  semaphore itself, and explicit tests for the filter and crash paths.
* **Fan-out/fan-in needs more than a counter.** When the DAG branches, one source dataset can
  become several downstream items across several terminal nodes, so a plain counter is wrong.
  This needs a lineage id per source row, refcounted, released at zero. The system-tag
  provenance machinery already carries per-row lineage, so the identifier exists — but this is
  meaningfully more work than the line

records.title: CachedFunctionPod cache hit ignores whether referenced output files still exist (dangling refs after intermediate deletion)
records.body:
## Summary

`CachedFunctionPod` treats a cache hit as valid based **solely on the input-data content hash**, without checking that the **output artifacts the cached record references** (`op.File` / `op.Directory` paths) still exist on disk. When those artifacts are deleted out-of-band (e.g. a scratch/hot-tier reclaim, TTL cleanup, or a manual `rm`), the pod still returns the stale record instead of recomputing. Downstream pods then receive a **dangling path reference** and fail at runtime with a confusing "file/namespace not found" error, when the correct behavior would be to invalidate the hit and recompute.

The root reason: what flows between pods is a **path reference** (an `op.File`/`engm://` string), not file bytes. Its content hash is stable whether or not the file exists, so deleting an intermediate is **invisible** to the lineage — nothing changes, so nothing triggers a rerun.

## Where

`orcapod/core/result_cache.py` — `CachedFunctionPod.lookup()`. It matches on `INPUT_DATA_HASH_COL` and returns the stored output `Data` directly:

```python
constraints = {constants.INPUT_DATA_HASH_COL: input_data.content_hash().to_prefixed_digest()}
result_table = self._result_database.get_records_with_column_value(...)
if result_table is None or result_table.num_rows == 0:
    return None
...
return Data(result_table, record_uuid=record_uuid,
            meta_info={self.RESULT_COMPUTED_FLAG: False})
```

There is no check that the paths inside `result_table` (for `op.File`/`op.Directory` columns) still resolve to existing artifacts.

## Minimal repro

```python
# Pod A writes a file and returns a REFERENCE to it
@function_pod
def preprocess(raw: Directory) -> {"ap_cache": File}:
    write_cache(cache_path)          # produces /cache/x
    return {"ap_cache": cache_path}

# Pod B consumes that reference
@function_pod
def motion(ap_cache: File) -> {"corrected": File}:
    rec = load(ap_cache)             # opens /cache/x

# Run 1: A computes, writes /cache/x, caches {input_hash -> ap_cache=/cache/x}
#        (B may or may not have completed)
# --- operator deletes /cache/x  (disk reclaim / TTL / manual rm) ---
# Run 2: A CACHE-HITS on input_hash -> returns /cache/x  (file NOT regenerated, no existence check)
#        B is a miss -> runs -> load('/cache/x') -> FileNotFoundError
```

**Expected:** In Run 2, A's cache hit is invalidated because `/cache/x` no longer exists → A recomputes → B succeeds.
**Actual:** A returns the dangling reference → B fails at runtime.

## Real-world impact

We hit this in the spike-sorting pipeline. A hot-tier cache reclaim deleted the intermediate caches of **23 partially-completed probes** (those that had passed `preprocess_ap` but not yet reached the terminal node). On the next run, `preprocess_ap` cache-hit and never regenerated the deleted binaries, so `correct_motion`/`sort` failed on missing inputs. There is currently **no way to force just those probes to recompute** short of DB surgery — the cache has no notion that the outputs are gone.

## Proposed fix

Add an opt-in existence check to `lookup()`:

- New flag, e.g. `verify_output_exists: bool` on `NodeConfig` / `CachedFunctionPod` (default `False` to preserve current performance).
- When enabled, after selecting the matching record and **before** returning it:
  1. Determine the output columns typed as `op.File` / `op.Directory` from the pod's output schema.
  2. For each referenced path, check existence via `UPath(path).exists()` — protocol-agnostic (works for local, `engm://`, `s3://`, …), no backend-specific code in core.
  3. If **any** referenced artifact is missing, log at INFO and `return None` (treat as a cache miss → recompute).

Sketch:

```python
if self._verify_output_exists:
    for path in _file_reference_paths(result_table, self._output_schema):
        if not UPath(path).exists():
            logger.info("Cache hit for %s references missing artifact %s; recomputing.",
                        constraints[constants.INPUT_DATA_HASH_COL], path)
            return None
```

### Design notes / trade-offs
- **Perf:** one `exists()` stat per file-reference column per cache hit. Existence-only (not re-hashing). For multi-root `engm://` namespaces this is a probe per root until found — hence opt-in, and worth documenting.
- **Partial outputs:** if any referenced artifact is missing, invalidate the whole record (a pod can't partially recompute its outputs).
- **Scope:** this is existence-only. A file that still exists but was *modified* out-of-band is **not** detected — that's a separate (content-integrity) concern and intentionally out of scope here.
- **Inline outputs:** non-file columns are skipped.

## Alternatives considered
- A runner-level `skip_cache_lookup` for a whole run — exists as a kwarg on `process()` but is not plumbed through executors, and it's coarse (forces recompute of everything in scope, including probes whose outputs are intact).
- Manual DB row deletion — no public per-record invalidation API; error-prone.

The existence-check approach is the smallest change that makes the cache **correct** in the presence of out-of-band artifact deletion, and it self-heals reclaims automatically.

records.title: Add CI caching for Rust and pnpm dependencies
records.body:
> 🟢 **Difficulty:** SIMPLE · **Area:** DevOps · **Estimated effort:** 2–6 hours

## 📌 Summary

Reduce CI duration with scoped dependency caches that preserve reproducibility.

## 🎯 Context & motivation

The repository runs multiple toolchains and can avoid repeated downloads without caching build outputs unsafely.

## 🛠 Scope of work

1. Measure current dependency install time.
2. Add lockfile-keyed caches.
3. Document cache invalidation behavior.

## 📁 Files to touch

| Path | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `.github/workflows` | Add dependency caching to relevant workflows. |
| `.github/workflows/README.md` | Document cache keys. |

_Paths are the expected shape of the change — if you need to deviate, explain why in the PR description._

## ✔️ Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cache keys include dependency lockfiles and toolchain inputs.
- [ ] A cache miss still produces a clean build.
- [ ] No credentials are cached.

## 🧪 Testing requirements

- [ ] Run workflows on a cache miss and hit.
- [ ] Verify dependency changes invalidate caches.

## ✅ CI requirements (non-negotiable)

**Every** check on your pull request must be green before review. Nothing is
merged on a red or skipped-because-broken pipeline.

| Pipeline | Runs when you touch | Must pass |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Frontend CI` (`.github/workflows/frontend.yml`) | `apps/frontend/**` | install → `npm run lint` → `tsc --noEmit` → `npm run test` → `vite build` → artifact upload |
| `Backend CI` (`.github/workflows/backend.yml`) | `apps/backend/**`, `packages/**`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | install (pnpm) → `prisma generate` → `pnpm run lint` → `tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` → `pnpm run test` → `pnpm run build`, plus the `Shared packages build` job |
| `Contracts CI` (`.github/workflows/contracts.yml`) | `contracts/**` | `cargo fmt --all --check` → `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` (with `RUSTFLAGS: -D warnings`, so **zero warnings**) → `cargo test --workspace` → `cargo build --workspace --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` |

Reproduce locally before pushing:

```bash
# frontend
cd apps/frontend && npm install && npm run lint && npx tsc --noEmit && npx vite build

# backend + shared packages
pnpm install && pnpm lint && pnpm build && pnpm test:all

# contracts
cd contracts && cargo fmt --all --check \
  && cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings \
  && cargo test --workspace \
  && cargo build --workspace --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
```

Also required:

- [ ] Branch name follows `CONTRIBUTING.md` (`feat/…`, `fix/…`, `chore/…`, `docs/…`, `refactor/…`).
- [ ] Commits use Conventional Commits with the correct scope (e.g. `feat(backend): …`).
- [ ] `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` filled in completely, screenshots for any UI change.
- [ ] At least **1 approving review**; branch is up to date with `main`.
- [ ] No generated artifacts, `.env` files, secrets, or lockfile churn unrelated to your change.


## 🧭 How to work on this

1. Comment on this issue to get it assigned — please don't open a PR for an
   unassigned issue.
2. Fork + branch from an up-to-date `main`.
3. Read `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `README.md` first; keep the change scoped to one
   domain (`apps/backend`, `apps/frontend`, `contracts`, `packages`, `ml`).
4. Keep the PR reviewable: if it grows past ~600 changed lines, split it and say
   so in the description.
5. Push early as a **draft PR** if you want directional feedback.


## 💬 Definition of done

PR merged into `main` with all acceptance criteria ticked, all CI pipelines green, docs updated where behaviour changed, and no follow-up work left undocumented (open a new issue for anything you deliberately defer).

records.title: ProjectBlockRegistry: add shared block directories with recursive scan
records.body:
## Description

Enhance `ProjectBlockRegistry` to support **shared block directories** with recursive scanning, enabling multi-module projects to share common blocks (glossary, references, trainers, exercise templates) from a single source of truth.

Currently, `ProjectBlockRegistry` scans only its own `blocks_dir` (flat, non-recursive). Projects with multiple modules that need to share blocks (e.g., a training with `ai4se6d_genai_intro`, `ai4se6d_vibecoding`, `ai4se6d_gensem` sharing a glossary) must duplicate block files across modules, leading to definition drift and maintenance burden.

## Motivation

**Real-world problem encountered**: A 6-day training project has 3 modules that each need the same glossary, trainer profile slides, and reference bibliography blocks. Despite creating a `shared-blocks/blocks/` directory with a shared glossary (`bck_shared_glossary.py`), the `ProjectBlockRegistry` cannot discover it. Each module ended up with its own `bck_glossary.py` with **diverging definitions** of the same terms (e.g., VibeCoding defined as "pair programmer" in one module and "without closely reviewing" in another).

The `setup.py` convention already adds `shared-blocks/` to `sys.path`, and `book.py` already adds `shared-blocks/static/` to static sources via `set_static_sources()`. Block sharing is the missing piece.

**Use cases**:
1. **Intra-project sharing** (immediate): Multiple modules in a training share glossary, references, trainer profiles
2. **Inter-project sharing** (future): A library of reusable block templates installed as a Python package
3. **Organized shared blocks**: Shared blocks organized in subdirectories by theme (`closing/`, `trainers/`, `exercises/`)

## Proposed Solution

### 1. New constructor parameters

```python
class ProjectBlockRegistry:
    def __init__(
        self,
        blocks_dir: Path,
        shared: list[Path] | None = None,   # Explicit shared directories
        auto_shared: bool = True,            # Auto-detect convention dir
    ):
```

- `shared`: explicit list of additional directories to scan for `bck_*.py` files
- `auto_shared` (default `True`): automatically detect `blocks_dir.parent.parent / "shared-blocks" / "blocks"` if it exists. **ON by default** because the convention already exists (`setup.py` adds `shared-blocks/` to `sys.path`, `book.py` adds `shared-blocks/static/` to static sources).

### 2. Resolution priority (first match wins)

```
1. Local blocks_dir (project's own blocks/)
2. Explicit shared dirs (in order given)
3. Auto-detected shared-blocks/blocks/ (convention)
```

A local block with the same name as a shared block **shadows** it (local wins).

### 3. Recursive scan (`rglob`)

Replace `glob("bck_*.py")` with `rglob("bck_*.py")` for **all** directories (local and shared). This enables subdirectory organization:

```
shared-blocks/blocks/
  closing/
    bck_shared_glossary.py
    bck_shared_references.py
  trainers/
    bck_trainer_ng.py
    bck_trainer_ts.py
  exercises/
    bck_exercise_template.py
```

All discovered as `blocks.bck_shared_glossary`, `blocks.bck_trainer_ng`, etc. — subdirectories are organizational, not namespacing.

**Exclusion**: Files inside `_atomic/` subdirectories are skipped (already loaded explicitly by composite blocks via `load_atomic_block()`).

### 4. Name collision handling: warning + first wins

If two `bck_*.py` files in different subdirectories share the same `stem`, log a warning and keep the first one found (deterministic via `sorted()`):

```python
logger.warning(
    "Block name collision: '%s' found in both '%s' and '%s'. Keeping first occurrence.",
    name, existing_path, new_path,
)
```

### 5. Enriched manifest

```python
manifest[name] = {
    "path": str(path),
    "loaded": False,
    "type": "composite" | "atomic",
    "source": "local" | "shared",           # NEW
    "source_dir": str(source_directory),     # NEW
    "subdirectory": "trainers" | None,       # NEW — relative subdir or None if root
    "shadows": str(shadowed_path) | None,    # NEW — path of shadowed shared block
}
```

### 6. New/updated public methods

```python
# Updated — new optional filter
def list_blocks(self, block_type=None, source=None) -> list:
    """Filter by type ('atomic'/'composite') and/or source ('local'/'shared')."""

# New
def get_source(self, block_name: str) -> str:
    """Return 'local' or 'shared'."""

# New
def get_shared_dirs(self) -> list[Path]:
    """Return the resolved shared directories (explicit + auto-detected)."""

# Updated — new fields
def get_stats(self) -> dict:
    """Now includes 'local', 'shared', 'shadowed' counts."""

# Updated — shows shared_dirs count
def __repr__(self) -> str
```

### 7. Internal refactoring

Extract a reusable `_scan_directory(directory, source)` method used by `_build_manifest()` for both local and shared dirs:

```python
def _scan_directory(self, directory: Path, source: str) -> Dict[str, dict]:
    """Scan a directory recursively for bck_*.py files, skipping _atomic/."""
    composites = self._detect_composites_in(directory)
    found = {}
    for path in sorted(directory.rglob("bck_*.py")):
        if "_atomic" in path.parts:
            continue
        name = path.stem
        if name in found:
            logger.warning(
                "Block name collision: '%s' in '%s' and '%s'. Keeping first.",
                name, found[name]["path"], path,
            )
            continue
        found[name] = {
            "path": str(path),
            "loaded": False,
            "type": "composite" if name in composites else "atomic",
            "source": source,
            "source_dir": str(directory),
            "subdirectory": str(path.parent.relative_to(directory)) if path.parent != directory else None,
        }
    return found
```

Extract `_detect_composites_in(directory)` as a `@staticmethod` (currently `_detect_composites` is hardcoded to `self.blocks_dir`).

| File | Changes |
|------|---------|
| `stre

records.title: Unprivileged DoS via cyclic NestedClass metadata in .NET PE parsing (infinite loop) in the eBPF profiler
records.body:
> Downgraded from security advisory GHSA-q99m-mcfv-2m95. Identifying details have been removed. @jmacd reviewed the original issue and [determined that a security response is not required](https://github.com/open-telemetry/sig-security/blob/main/security-response.md).


# Unprivileged DoS via cyclic `NestedClass` metadata in .NET PE parsing (infinite loop / OOM)

- **Severity:** Medium (Denial of Service) — same class as CVE-2026-48496
- **CVSS v3.1:** 6.2 — `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`
- **CWE:** CWE-835 (Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition / infinite loop) + CWE-400 (uncontrolled resource consumption — unbounded string growth)
- **Affected component:** `interpreter/dotnet/pe.go` — `resolveMethodName()` enclosing-class walk (lines 1251–1257); `NestedClass` table parse (lines 877–889) validates indices but permits cycles.
- **Affected version:** `open-telemetry/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler` @ `v0.0.202623-52-g692d5e3` (current `main`).
- **Confidence:** High (cycle constructibility and the un-capped loop confirmed by code; PoC demonstrates non-termination of the exact loop).

## Summary

When symbolizing a .NET frame, `resolveMethodName()` builds the fully-qualified
type name by walking the chain of enclosing classes:

```go
typeSpec := &pi.typeSpecs[idx]
for typeSpec.enclosingClass != 0 {
    enclosingSpec := &pi.typeSpecs[typeSpec.enclosingClass-1]
    typeName = fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", lookup(enclosingSpec.typeNameIdx), typeName)
    typeSpec = enclosingSpec
}
```

The `enclosingClass` links come from the PE's `NestedClass` metadata table. Parse
time (pe.go:877–889) validates that both `nestedClass` and `enclosingClass` are in
`[1, numTypeDefs]` — so the array indices are always in bounds (no OOB) — but it
does **not** forbid `enclosingClass == nestedClass` nor detect cycles, and the
walk loop has **no visited-set and no iteration cap**. A `NestedClass` row
`{nestedClass: 1, enclosingClass: 1}` sets `typeSpecs[0].enclosingClass = 1`, so
the loop steps from `typeSpecs[0]` to itself forever — an infinite loop that also
grows `typeName` without bound each iteration (CPU hang + memory exhaustion).

An unprivileged user running a .NET process with a crafted in-memory PE (or a
mapped crafted assembly) causes the profiler, upon symbolizing a sampled frame in
that process, to hang the symbolization worker and consume unbounded memory —
denial of service of the agent, the same impact class as CVE-2026-48496.

## Reachability (hop-by-hop)

1. **Attacker.** Unprivileged user runs a .NET workload whose loaded module's
   metadata (`NestedClass` table) it controls. ✔
2. **Parse accepts the cycle.** `NestedClass` rows are validated only for index
   range `[1, numTypeDefs]`; `enclosingClass == nestedClass` (self-cycle) and
   mutual cycles (A→B→A) pass. ✔
3. **Symbolization triggers the walk.** When the profiler samples a frame in the
   attacker's process and calls `resolveMethodName()`, the enclosing-class loop
   runs. With a cycle present it never reaches `enclosingClass == 0`. ✔ (no
   visited-set, no cap)
4. **Impact.** Infinite CPU loop in the symbolization path + unbounded
   `fmt.Sprintf` string growth → hang and OOM. No `recover()` in the path. ✔

## Root cause

The enclosing-class chain is treated as a guaranteed-acyclic, terminating list,
but it is attacker-controlled metadata. No cycle detection / depth bound and no
prohibition on self-reference.

## Proof of concept (benign, offline)

`findings/opentelemetry-ebpf-profiler/raw/poc_dotnet_cycle.go` faithfully
replicates the exact loop with a self-cyclic `typeSpecs` entry and a safety cap
(the real loop has none):

```
$ go run poc_dotnet_cycle.go
    [PoC] 5000000 iterations, enclosingClass still=1 (never 0): self-cycle, real loop has NO cap -> INFINITE HANG (DoS)
    [PoC] marker=OTEL-EBPF-003-dotnet-cycle — no visited-set; enclosingClass==nestedClass allowed (+unbounded typeName growth)
```

The PoC omits the per-iteration `fmt.Sprintf` growth purely to stay lightweight;
in the real code that growth additionally exhausts memory.

## CVSS v3.1 justification (6.2 — `AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H`)

Local unprivileged attacker (AV:L/PR:N), trivial crafting (AC:L), agent
hang/OOM (A:H), no confidentiality/integrity impact. Matches CVE-2026-48496.

## Adversarial re-read

- *"Indices are validated, so it's safe."* The validation prevents OOB but not
  cycles; the bug is non-termination, not a bad index.
- *"Cycles can't be constructed."* Refuted: parse validation allows
  `enclosingClass == nestedClass` and mutual references; both yield a cycle.
- *"A cap/visited-set exists."* Refuted: the loop body (pe.go:1253–1257) has
  neither.
- *"It needs the attacker's frame to be sampled."* True — it requires the profiler
  to symbolize a frame in the attacker's process; an attacker keeps their process
  on-CPU so it is sampled. This is the normal profiling path.
- Residual: Medium DoS (hang/OOM), not RCE.

## Remediation

Add cycle protection to the enclosing-class walk: track visited type-spec indices
(or impose a maximum nesting depth, e.g. 64) and break out on repeat/limit; also
reject `enclosingClass == nestedClass` at parse time. Defense-in-depth: bound
`typeName` length and wrap symbolization in `recover()`.
